analysis.one_liner: Bans drug companies from paying rivals to delay cheaper generic and biosimilar competition.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan bill to ban pay-for-delay drug settlements won unanimous committee approval but never received a House floor vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: When a brand-name drug company is sued by a generic or biosimilar maker, the two sometimes settle by exchanging money or other value for the generic maker's agreement to stay off the market for years — a "pay-for-delay" deal. This bill would let the Federal Trade Commission treat those deals as violations, with a presumption that any value-for-delay settlement is anticompetitive, and would impose penalties including forfeiting a generic's 180-day exclusivity. It also tightens the disclosure rules so side deals and verbal promises have to be filed with the FTC and Justice Department.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients and anyone who pays for prescription drugs, including employers and government health programs. Faster generic and biosimilar entry sharply lowers prices, and the bill is aimed at the settlements that keep cheaper versions off the market for years beyond what the patents would require.

how_it_helps.text: The bill lets the FTC bring an enforcement action against any settlement of a patent dispute over a drug in which the generic or biosimilar filer receives anything of value and agrees to delay its research, manufacture, marketing, or sales; such an agreement is presumed anticompetitive.

The presumption can only be overcome with clear and convincing evidence, and the bill bars the fact-finder from assuming that entry would not have happened until patent expiration — closing the arguments companies typically use to justify delay deals.

It requires company executives to certify, under penalty, that everything filed with the FTC and Justice Department includes the complete agreement, related side agreements, and written descriptions of any oral promises — targeting the undisclosed side deals that have historically accompanied these settlements.
Violators face civil penalties of up to three times the value gained, and a generic filer that violates the rule forfeits its valuable 180-day first-filer exclusivity period.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers, which would lose the ability to pay generic rivals to keep cheaper competition off the market and thereby extend years of monopoly-priced sales. Some generic and biosimilar makers would also lose the settlement payments they currently receive for staying out. In some cases the bill could mean fewer settlements overall, with brand companies litigating patent disputes to the end instead.

drawbacks.text: The bill could chill legitimate settlements. Because a settlement usually lets a generic reach the market before the patent expires, some fair settlements bring competition earlier; if companies fear liability under the bill's presumption, a brand firm may simply litigate the patent to the end, keeping a generic off the market for years longer than a settlement would have. The bill tries to manage this by exempting early-entry rights, capped litigation-cost payments (starting at $7.5 million a year), and covenants not to sue, and by allowing a procompetitive-benefits defense.

The scope is narrow. It addresses only value-for-delay patent settlements; it does not directly lower drug prices, cap prices, or change patent terms, so it leaves other major drivers of drug prices untouched.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real and well-documented: pay-for-delay deals keep cheaper drugs off the market for years, and the FTC's enforcement tools here are aimed squarely at that. The honest cost is the risk that some genuinely procompetitive early-entry settlements become harder to strike, which in some cases could delay generics slightly longer — though the bill's explicit exemptions for early entry, litigation costs, and covenants not to sue are designed to preserve those deals. On balance the design is careful rather than careless, and the potential savings to consumers and health payers outweigh the risk.

outcome.mechanism: The House Judiciary Committee approved it unanimously and put it on the House calendar on December 24, 2020, but the House never voted on it and the Congress ended ten days later.

narrative.text: Representative Jerrold Nadler introduced the bill on April 29, 2019, joined from the start by Republicans Doug Collins and Steve Cicilline's fellow members on the Judiciary Committee.
It was referred to the Judiciary Committee and the Energy and Commerce Committee on introduction day.
On April 30, 2019, the Judiciary Committee held a markup session and ordered the bill reported by voice vote — a unanimous approval with no recorded dissent.
The committee formally reported the bill on December 24, 2020 (H. Rept. 116-693, Part I); Energy and Commerce was discharged, and the bill was placed on the Union Calendar, Calendar No. 576.
No House floor vote ever took place before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021, so the bill died on the calendar despite unanimous committee approval and bipartisan sponsorship.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug makers keep the option of paying generic rivals to stay off the market, preserving extended periods of monopoly-priced sales on affected drugs. Patients and health payers continue to bear the higher prices that these settlements sustain.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Brand-name drug makers keeping delay deals

sides.party_line_note: The bill was bipartisan from the start: a Democratic chairman introduced it with the top Republican on the Judiciary Committee, 4 cosponsors split evenly between parties (2 of 197 House Republicans and 2 of 231 House Democrats), and the committee reported it by voice vote with no dissent.

industries.note: The bill removes their ability to pay generic and biosimilar makers to delay entry, which today lets them collect years of additional monopoly-priced sales on drugs facing patent challenges. Those extra years of higher prices are paid directly by patients, employers, and government health programs.

Generic and biosimilar companies would lose the settlement payments some of them collect for staying off the market, but they gain from the bill's core goal: earlier market entry, which means more sales of lower-priced products. Their interest in selling cheap generics runs alongside patients' interest in access.
